tldr: This study uncovers a severe vulnerability when using vision-language models (VLMs) as reward functions for robotics: simply paraphrasing task instructions without changing their meaning drastically shifts evaluation scores, even flipping identical robot behavior between success and failure.
hero_caption: An illustration showing that for the exact same robot trajectory video, simply paraphrasing the instruction "Pick radish, then place in pink bowl" without altering its meaning causes a VLM to output contradictory rewards of score 1 (failure) and score 5 (complete success).
overview:
Using vision-language models (VLMs) to automatically evaluate robot task progress from images or videos based on natural language instructions has attracted significant attention, as it substantially reduces the manual effort of reward engineering for reinforcement learning. However, there has been an overlooked blind spot: does paraphrase invariance truly hold—meaning, should semantically equivalent goal descriptions yield identical rewards for the exact same robot trajectory?

Here, the authors discover that slightly rewording an instruction can lead state-of-the-art VLMs to judge the exact same behavior in completely opposite ways, flipping evaluations from complete success to complete failure. To systematically measure this issue, they introduce "ROBORMBENCH," a benchmark consisting of 2,390 real-robot trajectories and 21,673 strictly verified, semantically equivalent paraphrased instructions.

Evaluating a wide range of state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source VLMs reveals that paraphrase-induced reward contradictions are widespread and severe. Scaling up model parameters or adding explicit reasoning processes does not resolve this issue, and in some cases even makes it worse. In contrast, dedicated reward models trained directly with trajectory-grounded supervision demonstrate strong robustness. This important study makes it clear that designing reward models resilient to superficial phrasing differences is indispensable for future robot learning.
contributions: Systematically uncovered for the first time that VLM reward models for robot trajectories are extremely fragile to meaning-preserving paraphrases, even reversing success and failure judgments for identical behavior.
Introduced and publicly released "ROBORMBENCH," a benchmark comprising 2,390 real-robot trajectories and 21,673 verified paraphrased instructions across three tiers of linguistic divergence.

Defined robustness metrics, including the Score Crossing Rate (SCR) which captures contradictory failure vs. success judgments on the same trajectory, and comprehensively evaluated state-of-the-art VLMs.

Demonstrated that model scaling and explicit reasoning do not solve paraphrase fragility, whereas dedicated reward models supervised on trajectory data and variance-reduction training prove highly effective.

sections.heading: Can Changing Just Phrasing Turn "Success" into "Failure"? An Overlooked Pitfall in Reward Models
sections.summary: In language-conditioned robot reinforcement learning, using VLMs as reward functions (progress evaluators) is rapidly growing. However, rewording instructions with synonyms or different sentence structures produces contradictory reward predictions, revealing a severe problem that substantially degrades the quality of downstream trajectory selection.
sections.details:
Natural language is the most intuitive and scalable interface for tasking robots. In recent years, significant research has focused on vision-language models (VLMs) that take robot trajectories (camera videos) and goal texts as inputs to predict task completion as continuous progress scores, such as from 1 to 5. This approach avoids the need to hand-craft dense rewards and provides fine-grained intermediate progress feedback, making it exceptionally convenient for RL policy optimization.

However, reward model instability is fatal in reinforcement learning. Because RL algorithms explore and update policies based on reward magnitudes, feeding inconsistent rewards for identical robot behaviors depending merely on phrasing confuses the learning signal. As a result, learning can stall or lead to reward hacking, where policies overfit to specific linguistic habits rather than accomplishing the actual objective.

Conventional evaluation benchmarks evaluated models using only a single canonical instruction, leaving this fragility overlooked. To address this, the authors introduce "ROBORMBENCH," a benchmark that holds the robot trajectory fixed and comprehensively provides synonymous instructions to evaluate reward consistency. Experiments confirmed that for certain general-purpose VLMs, simply shifting the perspective of an instruction reverses success/failure judgments on more than half of the benchmark's trajectories. Furthermore, in offline trajectory selection (best-of-$N$), models with higher paraphrase-induced contradictions consistently select lower-quality trajectories.

captions.F1: A concrete example of the problem raised in this study. Instruction 1, "Pick radish, then place in pink bowl," and Instruction 2, "After picking radish, place in pink bowl," carry the exact same meaning, yet the model assigns contradictory extreme rewards (1 and 5) to the identical robot trajectory.

sections.heading: The State of Robot RL, LLM Reward Models, and VLM Reward Functions
sections.summary: Designing reward functions in robot RL has long been a challenge, and automated reward engineering leveraging LLM and VLM knowledge has advanced rapidly. However, risks similar to the biases and hacking observed in text-generation reward models have remained unexamined in robot VLM reward functions.
sections.details:
This paper builds on three primary lines of research:

- Advances in Robot Reinforcement Learning (RL):
Applying RL to physical robots has a long history, but due to the challenges of real-world trial and error, sim-to-real transfer of policies trained in simulation has long been the dominant paradigm. Recently, with advances in hardware and algorithms, researchers have increasingly trained locomotion and manipulation directly on physical systems, or adapted and fine-tuned large-scale generalist robot policies in real environments. However, these systems still rely on hand-crafted reward functions or explicit human feedback.

- Reward Models for Language Models:
Reward models are essential in LLM post-training (such as RLHF), and benchmarks like RewardBench have meticulously evaluated model accuracy and biases. Evaluations of multimodal reward models have also progressed, but vulnerabilities to stylistic biases and reward hacking remain significant hurdles.

- The Emergence of VLM Reward Models for Robotics:
Leveraging the rich commonsense knowledge and spatial reasoning of VLMs, numerous studies evaluate robot task progress from videos or image pairs. Yet most prior work evaluated models against single goal instructions, entirely overlooking the perspective of paraphrase robustness—namely, how rewards fluctuate when humans slightly rephrase an instruction.

sections.heading: Designing RoboRMBench: A Benchmark to Measure Paraphrase Robustness
sections.summary: The authors paired 2,390 real-robot trajectories with 21,673 verified paraphrased instructions across three linguistic tiers: lexical substitution, syntactic restructuring, and perspective shifts. They also established new evaluation metrics, including the Score Crossing Rate (SCR), which captures failure vs. success flips on identical behaviors.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Let $\tau$ be a robot trajectory, and $G(\tau) = \{g_1, \ldots, g_K\}$ be a set of semantically equivalent goal instructions. The progress score $r_k = R_\theta(\tau, g_k)$ output by a reward model $R_\theta$ should remain constant across any paraphrase $g_k$ in the set, provided the video $\tau$ and task intent remain unchanged. RoboRMBench directly tests this paraphrase invariance property.

### 3.2 Dataset Construction Methodology
As the base dataset, the authors adopted "RoboRewardBench," which features diverse manipulation behaviors collected across 14 distinct physical robot platforms. To mitigate label imbalance from the original data, they downsampled the dataset so scores 1 through 5 are evenly distributed. Paraphrases were generated using three strategies spanning different levels of linguistic divergence:
- Lexical Substitution (LS): Replacing nouns or verbs with synonyms (e.g., "put" $\rightarrow$ "place").
- Syntactic Restructuring (SR): Altering sentence structure while preserving meaning (e.g., passivization, reordering clauses).
- Action-Goal Perspective Shift (AGPS): Rewriting action-centric descriptions into outcome-centric ones, or vice versa (e.g., "put the block in the box" $\rightarrow$ "aim for the block to be inside the box").

To prevent semantic drift, strict filtering was conducted using an ensemble of three independent LLMs (Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek). Any candidate flagged by even a single model for introducing minor nuance shifts (such as adverbs like "slowly") was discarded. Human validation on 210 samples confirmed a 96% recall in catching semantic deviations. The final benchmark consists of 2,390 trajectories and 21,673 verified paraphrases.

### 3.3 Evaluation Protocol and Metrics
To evaluate both robustness and accuracy, three metrics were introduced:
- Score Crossing Rate (SCR): The proportion of trajectories where, for the same trajectory, one paraphrase predicts a failure-level score (1–2) while another predicts a success-level score (4–5), crossing the success threshold. This reflects an absolute contradiction rate independent of a reference sentence.
- Flip Rate (FR): The fraction of individual paraphrases where the success/failure judgment flips relative to the original canonical instruction.
- Mean Error (ME): The mean absolute error between the average predicted score across all paraphrases and the ground-truth human progress label (measuring pure predictive accuracy).

captions.F2: The dataset construction and evaluation pipeline of RoboRMBench. Paraphrased instructions are generated from original instructions using three strategies (lexical substitution, syntactic restructuring, and action-goal perspective shifts), rigorously vetted via an LLM ensemble, and fed to models to compute SCR, FR, and ME.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: State-of-the-Art VLMs Struggle While Dedicated Reward Models Excel
sections.summary: Many state-of-the-art commercial and open-source VLMs are highly fragile to paraphrasing, and neither scaling up model size nor introducing reasoning solves the problem. Conversely, dedicated models trained on trajectory data and approaches incorporating variance-reduction penalties during training demonstrate strong robustness.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation included GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Gemini (2.5 flash-lite, 2.5 flash, 3-flash), Claude (haiku-4.5, sonnet-4.6), the Qwen3-vl series, the Gemma3 series, and the Llama4 series, along with "RoboReward (RR-4B, RR-8B)," dedicated robot reward models fine-tuned on trajectory data.

### 4.2 Key Experimental Findings
- Severe Instability in General-Purpose VLMs:
Under perspective shifts (AGPS), models like Gemini2.5-flash-lite and Llama4-scout exceeded an SCR of 0.5. In other words, for more than half of the exact same behaviors, the verdict swung between "success" and "failure" based purely on phrasing. Furthermore, as linguistic structures diverged—moving from lexical substitutions (LS) to syntactic restructuring (SR) and perspective shifts (AGPS)—both SCR and FR consistently deteriorated.

- Superior Robustness of Dedicated Reward Models:
In contrast, RR-4B and RR-8B, trained directly for reward prediction on robot trajectories, achieved an exceptionally low SCR of 0.034 on LS and kept SCR below 0.12 even on the challenging AGPS split. This substantially outperformed frontier commercial models with vastly larger parameter counts.

- The Divergence Between Accuracy and Robustness:
Some models showed low Mean Error (ME) yet were fragile to paraphrases (e.g., Gemini3-flash had a high-accuracy ME of 0.681 on LS, but was unstable with SCR=0.271), while others produced consistently biased predictions that nonetheless stayed stable across paraphrases. This demonstrates that accuracy and robustness are distinct dimensions requiring separate evaluation.

### 4.3 In-Depth Analysis (Scaling, Reasoning, and Downstream Policy Impact)
- Scale and Reasoning Are Not Silver Bullets:
Increasing model size did not lower SCR; in fact, larger models sometimes became overly sensitive to surface-level differences, worsening the rate. Similarly, enabling explicit reasoning (thinking processes) increased SCR in Qwen and Gemini rather than stabilizing outputs.
- Direct Negative Impact on Policy Improvement:
In an offline best-of-$N$ trajectory selection experiment choosing the single highest-reward trajectory out of 20 candidates, models with lower SCR (higher paraphrase robustness) correctly selected trajectories with higher true progress and significantly reduced regret relative to the best trajectory, even when Mean Error (ME) was comparable (correlation coefficient $r=0.882$).

### 4.4 Mitigating Fragility
Averaging predictions over multiple generated paraphrases at test time ("Paraphrase Aggregation") steadily reduced SCR, but increased API inference costs. In contrast, applying "Variance Reduction Training," which adds a regularization term penalizing score variance across paraphrased prompts during training, dramatically improved both SCR and ME without adding any inference overhead.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Building Robot Reward Models Resilient to Phrasing Variations
sections.summary: This work demonstrates a severe vulnerability in using VLMs as reward functions: paraphrasing instructions can flip evaluations of identical behavior between polar opposites. Achieving truly reliable robot RL requires designing consistent, trajectory-grounded reward models rather than simply pursuing larger model scale.
sections.details:
This study shines a light on the unexamined challenge of paraphrase fragility when deploying vision-language models as robot reward functions.

The key takeaway from the comprehensive evaluation on RoboRMBench is that advanced language understanding, vast parameter counts, and chain-of-thought reasoning in generalist VLMs cannot resolve this oversensitivity to superficial text variations. On the contrary, this fragility directly causes models to favor incorrect behaviors during downstream trajectory selection.

At the same time, the paper shows that training dedicated reward models with trajectory grounding and introducing variance-reduction loss functions are remarkably effective. Paraphrase robustness must become an essential evaluation axis in the ongoing development of robot foundation models and natural language interfaces.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind Data Filtering and Verification of API Determinism
sections.summary: The appendix provides detailed analyses supporting the paper's claims, including concrete examples of conservative paraphrase filtering, experiments isolating API stochasticity from genuine paraphrase fragility, and a more extreme success-flip metric (ESCR).
sections.details:
The appendix provides important verification results that reinforce the main claims:

- Validity of Conservative Filtering:
Most rejected paraphrase candidates were grammatically sound and fluent, but introduced slight changes to elements directly tied to robot reward evaluation, such as object attributes (color or shape), manipulation verbs, spatial relationships, or temporal/speed constraints. Because avoiding the risk of retaining semantically shifted sentences is paramount when assessing robustness, this strict pruning proved well-justified.

- Distinguishing Paraphrase Fragility from API Randomness:
To separate sampling stochasticity in commercial APIs from paraphrase-induced variance, an experiment repeated identical prompts and images 10 times. The standard deviation across repeated runs of the identical instruction averaged just 0.09, whereas the standard deviation across paraphrased instructions reached 0.52. This proves that the observed instability stems from the linguistic structure of the paraphrases rather than API stochastic noise.

- Presence of Extreme Contradictions (ESCR):
Even when filtering out subtle fluctuations near the boundary (such as shifts between scores 2 and 4) and focusing solely on polar-opposite contradictions between score 1 (complete failure) and score 5 (complete success) via "ESCR," many general-purpose VLMs still exhibited contradictions, confirming this as a fundamental flaw.

takeaways: When using VLMs as robot reward models, performance must not be evaluated on single instructions alone; stability against synonymous and syntactic paraphrases must be explicitly verified.
Model scaling and explicit reasoning processes do not resolve paraphrase fragility, and can even worsen performance by over-sensitizing models to superficial phrasing changes.

Rather than relying directly on general-purpose VLMs, adopting smaller dedicated models trained directly on robot trajectory data or penalizing paraphrase variance during training proves far more effective.
limitations: Generated and verified paraphrases are restricted entirely to English, leaving robustness in multilingual settings and code-switching unexamined.

Evaluations are limited to predicting episodic progress scores at trajectory completion, leaving behavior in other reward modeling regimes—such as per-step dense reward shaping or pairwise trajectory comparisons—unexplored.
Because paraphrases were generated and filtered using modern LLM ensembles, extremely subtle physical context mismatches that LLMs themselves fail to detect may still be present in minor amounts.
